entry.title: Checking collision metrics against the logged trajectory

link.title: Checking collision metrics against the logged trajectory

entry.content:
Experiment note · Occupancy world-model evaluation

An early version of the planning evaluator flagged the logged human trajectory as colliding on 1.9% of waypoints and off-road 12% of the time. Those rates prompted a closer look at how the checks mapped occupancy labels into violations.

A logged trajectory can contain real violations. Here, inspection exposed three problems in the evaluator itself.

Missing ground labels became off-road events

Occ3D does not observe the ground directly under the ego vehicle. The initial check treated an absent road label as evidence that the vehicle had left the road.

The corrected check requires a positively labeled non-drivable surface: sidewalk, terrain, vegetation, or other-flat. Missing data remains missing data. That distinction matters before comparing two planners, since both would otherwise inherit the same mislabeled events.

The body-height band included kerbs

The collision check looks for occupied voxels intersecting the vehicle’s body band. Kerbs and sloped road extended into the lowest cells used by the first implementation.

Moving the lower boundary to 0.6 m, with the band ending at 1.8 m, changed what counted as a body collision. A collision metric depends on this geometry as well as on the trajectory.

Stray labels appeared inside the ego box

About 2% of frames contained stray occupancy labels inside the ego vehicle’s own box. Ignoring those ego cells removed another source of false collision events.

These corrections are recorded in the project’s metric-fix commit. They change the evaluator, so planning comparisons need to use the corrected checks consistently.

What was compared afterward

The planning study keeps the same 32 candidate trajectories per scene and changes their scoring cost. Under its occupancy-based checks, obstacle collisions fell from 0.660% for the imitation prior to 0.386% with world-model scoring.

Saved planning comparison. See the repository for the rates, paired bootstrap results, and maneuver breakdown.

The inputs are ground-truth past occupancy, and the plans are evaluated on logged data. The voxel-based collision rates should be compared within this study. They use different observations and geometry from box-based rates reported elsewhere.

Checks worth carrying forward

Before interpreting a planning score, inspect what the evaluator does with an unobserved cell, a sloped surface, and a label inside the ego footprint. Then look at the scene slices: the aggregate collision improvement in this study coexists with a worse agent-collision result on left turns.

The left-turn slice contains 180 scenes. The repository has not ruled out a real regression in agent collisions.

Read the case study · Inspected evaluation record · Metric-fix commit
entry.summary: Three geometry and labeling issues that made an occupancy-based planning evaluation flag the logged human trajectory.

entry.title: Keeping tracks when stereo matching fails

link.title: Keeping tracks when stereo matching fails

entry.content:
Engineering note · Stereo VIO repository experiment

On EuRoC V2_03_difficult, the stereo front end sometimes delivered no features for two to seven seconds. The MSCKF continued on inertial measurements and accumulated error. The sliding-window estimator diverged.

The useful diagnostic was the difference between stereo matches and temporal tracks.

What disappeared, and what remained

The cameras expose independently. In dim parts of this sequence, cam0’s exposure exceeded 50 ms and its rate dropped to about 10 Hz. Its images became motion-blurred while cam1’s stayed sharp. Matching blurred patches to sharp ones failed, even with a 31×31 LK window and five pyramid levels.

Tracking cam0 against its previous frame still worked for about 60% of the corners. The front end was discarding these tracks because they lacked a right-camera match.

Saved diagnostic figure from the VIO repository. The plotted measurements are unchanged.

Keeping the observations took more than a flag

The revised front end keeps a cam0 track with a missing right-camera coordinate. A forward/backward tracking check must return within one pixel, since the stereo consistency check is unavailable.

The back ends also need to understand the reduced observation:

  • The MSCKF adds two image residual rows for a monocular observation, rather than four for stereo.
  • A feature with no stereo depth waits for 0.2 m of motion perpendicular to its viewing ray before MSCKF triangulation.
  • The sliding window triangulates a monocular landmark once the anchor and current rays are at least one degree apart, then uses cam0 reprojection factors.

The baseline check mattered. Without it, V2_01 diverged after the additional tracks were introduced.

The tradeoff across sequences

V2_03, ATE RMSE Stereo-only Final configuration
MSCKF 0.677 m 0.217 m
Sliding window Diverged 0.200 m

Keeping every available monocular track was not uniformly beneficial. These features compete with stereo tracks for grid slots. The final MSCKF configuration prunes cam0-only tracks first when a cell is full; the sliding window retains the unpruned variant.

Those choices were selected on the same 11 EuRoC sequences used for evaluation. The comparison establishes the behavior of these configurations on that benchmark; a separate dataset is needed to assess how well the choice transfers.

The remaining question is how to choose the mixture of stereo and monocular observations as match quality changes. The present grid policy is a heuristic, and the two back ends prefer different variants.

Read the case study · Inspected implementation and experiment record
entry.summary: Why cam0-only tracks helped a stereo VIO system on EuRoC V2_03, and why retaining them also needed triangulation checks.
